title: Defying Gravity: The Extraordinary Science Behind High Jump and Pole Vault
summary: Clearing a bar nearly three metres in the air using only a fibreglass pole, or jumping over two metres using only your body — these are among sport's most technically demanding feats. We look at the physics and artistry behind athletics' vertical events.
content:
When Dick Fosbury arrived at the 1968 Mexico City Olympics and cleared the high jump bar by going over it backwards — head first, arching his back, letting his legs trail over last — the crowd was baffled. Officials checked the rulebook. His technique, which became known as the Fosbury Flop, was entirely legal. And it was so obviously superior to every existing technique that within a decade it had replaced them all.

Today, every elite high jumper uses the Fosbury Flop. The technique allows a jumper to clear a bar that is actually higher than their own centre of mass — the bar can pass below the arc of the body even as the body passes over it. It is a beautiful example of how a single insight can permanently change a sport.

The Physics of the High Jump

The high jump is a conversion of horizontal speed into vertical height. The approach run — usually a curved arc of 10-12 strides — allows the jumper to build momentum that is then redirected upward at the point of takeoff. The curve of the approach creates centrifugal force that helps with the rotation needed to execute the Flop.

The world record, set by Javier Sotomayor in 1993 at 2.45 metres, has stood for over three decades — the longest-standing world record in men's field events. What makes it so hard to break? Partly physiology — the ideal high jumper is tall, with long legs and enormous spring. Partly the difficulty of converting speed to height efficiently enough to consistently approach the absolute limits of human capability.

High jumping is not about jumping high. It is about falling efficiently — arranging your body so that every part of it clears the bar with the minimum possible margin.

Pole Vault: The Most Technical Event in Athletics

If the high jump is elegant, the pole vault is extraordinary. The athlete runs at speed, plants a fibreglass pole in a metal box, and uses the pole's elastic energy — stored as it bends under their weight — to catapult themselves over a bar nearly six metres in the air.

The sequence of movements required — the grip, the plant, the swing-up, the inversion, the push-off, the bar clearance — must all be executed in approximately one second. Any error in the chain, and the bar comes down. The world record of 6.21 metres, set by Armand Duplantis, represents the most remarkable feat of human athletic achievement — a man propelling himself to nearly twice his own height using a stick.

Duplantis and the New Era

Armand Duplantis has broken the pole vault world record so many times that it has become almost routine. His combination of exceptional technique, extraordinary athleticism, and a seemingly limitless ceiling for improvement has made him the most dominant athlete in his discipline since Sergey Bubka's era of the 1980s and 90s.

How high can he go? The theoretical limit of human pole vaulting, based on current physics and physiology, is estimated at somewhere around 6.4-6.5 metres. Duplantis appears to be heading there, one centimetre at a time.
